patient.name: Kwame Asante
patient.setting: Diabetic foot clinic, then Emergency Department
patient.complaint: Two black toes on the right foot, now smelly and swollen
background: Type 2 diabetes for 20 years, poorly controlled
Lives alone in Tottenham; no known drug allergies

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a black or discoloured limb: dry, wet or gas gangrene is decided by moisture, demarcation, infection and crepitus.

points: Kwame, 67, has **two black toes** on his right foot.
They turned dark over 3 weeks and **stopped hurting**.
They are dry, shrivelled and hard.
A **sharp line** separates black toes from pink skin.

steps.lead: Kwame's toes have died from **ischaemia**: diabetes, PVD and smoking are all on his list of risk factors.

steps.q: Kwame's toes are dry, black, painless and clearly demarcated, with no fever. Which type of gangrene?
steps.r: Mummified, painless, **clear demarcation**, no infection: **dry gangrene** from chronic arterial insufficiency.

points: He misses his follow-up; 10 days later he attends ED.
The foot is **swollen, red and moist**, with blisters.
**Pus** and a foul smell; severe pain.
No clear edge between dead and living tissue.

steps.lead: Kwame started with **dry** gangrene; infection has now turned it **wet**: painful, moist, foul, febrile and poorly demarcated.

steps.title: Dry vs wet vs gas gangrene
head: Feature
Dry
Wet
Gas

steps.lead: Kwame has no wound, no crepitus and no gas, so this is not **gas gangrene**: that follows trauma and crackles under your fingers.

steps.text: **Pain out of proportion** plus crepitus after a minor cut is gas gangrene (or necrotising infection), not cellulitis. Oral antibiotics are never the answer.

steps.lead: Kwame's fever, tachycardia and low BP warn of the feared complications: **sepsis**, multi-organ failure and amputation.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (ABPI for dry gangrene), the gold standard to find the blockage (CT angiography), and X-ray for gas in soft tissue.

steps.lead: In clinic, Kwame's toes were examined for **viability** and his ABPI was measured to judge the arterial supply.

visual.title: Kwame's right ABPI
visual.label: Kwame 0.38
visual.caption: An ABPI **below 0.8** supports dry gangrene from arterial disease; 0.38 is critical.

steps.text: Diabetics can have stiff, calcified arteries that give a **falsely high** ABPI. Absent pulses with a 'normal' ABPI still need imaging.

steps.title: Kwame's bloods in ED
steps.text: Raised CRP, WCC and lactate: wet gangrene with sepsis and acute kidney injury.

visual.title: Lactate
visual.label: Kwame 4.1
visual.caption: Lactate above 4 means septic shock risk: resuscitate now.

steps.lead: Once stable, **CT angiography** maps Kwame's blockage. In suspected gas gangrene you would also check CRP, lactate and **X-ray for gas**.

steps.text: **ABPI** first, **CT angiography** for the blockage, **X-ray** for gas in the soft tissues. Never delay surgery in gas gangrene to get a scan.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': urgent vascular referral for dry gangrene, IV antibiotics plus surgical review for wet, and emergency debridement for gas gangrene.

steps.q: Kwame is febrile, hypotensive and has wet gangrene. What comes first?
o: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and urgent surgical review
steps.r: Wet gangrene is an **emergency**: Sepsis Six with immediate IV antibiotics and urgent surgery. Imaging can wait.

steps.lead: Kwame gets IV **co-amoxiclav** now plus an urgent surgical review. Had this been gas gangrene: emergency debridement, **piperacillin-tazobactam** and ICU.

steps.title: Gangrene management by type
nodes: Dry → urgent vascular referral for revascularisation
Wet → IV co-amoxiclav (or fluclox + metronidazole) + urgent surgery
Gas → emergency debridement + IV pip-taz + ICU
steps.caption: The wetter and more systemic, the faster you operate.

steps.lead: Kwame's infected, non-viable toes need **surgical debridement** and amputation: dead tissue will not recover with antibiotics alone.

visual.title: Kwame after IV antibiotics and amputation
visual.caption: Source control in theatre plus IV antibiotics settles the sepsis.

steps.lead: Back at the dry-gangrene stage, Kwame needed an **urgent vascular referral** for revascularisation, plus **clopidogrel** and **atorvastatin** lifelong.

steps.text: Do not reach for **oral** antibiotics or an outpatient referral when the stem has fever, moist necrosis or crepitus. That is wet or gas gangrene: IV and theatre.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the organism and toxin in gas gangrene, why dry gangrene is demarcated, and what the ABPI ratio reflects.

steps.lead: Kwame's toes first died from critically low blood supply (**ischaemic, dry** gangrene); bacteria then colonised the dead tissue (**wet**).
Kwame's original sharp line formed because nearby skin stayed **perfused**; infection destroyed that boundary and spread.

steps.q: Which toxin explains the crepitus and myonecrosis of gas gangrene?
steps.r: **Clostridium perfringens alpha-toxin**, a lecithinase, destroys cell membranes, causing myonecrosis and gas in tissue planes.

steps.lead: Kwame had no gas gangrene, but in that case **alpha-toxin** destroys muscle and makes gas, so tissue crackles and hurts beyond what you see.
Kwame's ABPI of 0.38 means his ankle pressure is little more than a third of his arm pressure: **severe ischaemia**.

mcq.q: Which feature is typical of dry gangrene?
mcq.r: Dry gangrene is mummified, painless and **clearly demarcated**.

mcq.q: What is the classic palpation finding in gas gangrene?
mcq.r: **Crepitus** from gas in the soft tissues (subcutaneous emphysema).
Wet gangrene is infected necrotic tissue: moist, painful, foul, febrile, **no demarcation**.

mcq.q: Which ABPI value supports dry gangrene from arterial disease?
What is the gold standard to identify the arterial blockage?
mcq.r: **CT angiography** maps the blockage before revascularisation.

mcq.q: What is first-line antibiotic for wet gangrene in the notes?
mcq.r: **IV co-amoxiclav**, or flucloxacillin plus metronidazole, with urgent surgical review.

mcq.q: What is the key treatment for gas gangrene?
mcq.r: **Emergency debridement**, IV piperacillin-tazobactam and ICU care.

mcq.q: What does Clostridium perfringens alpha-toxin do?
o: Destroys cell membranes as a lecithinase
mcq.r: Alpha-toxin is a **lecithinase** causing myonecrosis and gas production.

prompts.q: What is gangrene and what are its risk factors?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ischaemia first, infection second.

points.p: Tissue death due to ischaemia, sometimes with superimposed infection
points.why: Infection is what turns dry into wet.
Smoking is specific for dry gangrene of the toes.

prompts.q: Describe the presentation of dry gangrene.

points.p: Chronic arterial insufficiency, ischaemia alone, no infection

points.why: The key difference from wet gangrene.

prompts.q: Describe the presentation of wet gangrene.
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: wet = infected and an emergency.

points.p: Infection within necrotic tissue; an emergency

points.why: Moisture comes from infection and tissue liquefaction.

prompts.q: What is gas gangrene, what causes it and what are the classic findings?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: trauma + crepitus + pain out of proportion.

points.p: Clostridial myonecrosis caused by Clostridium perfringens
Follows trauma, e.g. a minor cut
Pain out of proportion to findings
points.why: Same red flag as necrotising fasciitis.

points.p: Foul discharge, bullae, discolouration, systemic infection

prompts.q: How do you investigate dry gangrene?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: bedside first, then map the arteries.

points.why: Can be falsely high in diabetes.

points.p: CT angiography: gold standard to identify the blockage

prompts.q: How do you investigate suspected gas gangrene?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: tests must not delay theatre.

points.p: X-ray showing gas in the soft tissues

prompts.q: How do you manage dry, wet and gas gangrene?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one plan per type.

points.p: Dry: urgent vascular surgery referral for revascularisation
points.why: Restore flow if tissue can be saved.

points.p: Wet: immediate IV co-amoxiclav (or flucloxacillin + metronidazole) and urgent surgical review
Gas: IV piperacillin-tazobactam (vancomycin/meropenem alternatives) and ICU

prompts.q: Why is dry gangrene demarcated while wet gangrene spreads?

points.p: Dry: tissue mummifies as it desiccates
points.why: Desiccated tissue shrinks and turns black.

points.p: Adjacent viable tissue stays perfused, giving a clear line
points.why: The demarcation is the edge of the blood supply.

points.p: Wet: bacteria produce toxins and gas, liquefying tissue

prompts.q: Why does gas gangrene cause crepitus and disproportionate pain, and what does ABPI measure?

points.p: Myonecrosis and gas in tissue planes
ABPI: ratio of ankle to brachial systolic BP, falls with stenosis

glossary.gangrene: Death of body tissue from loss of blood supply, sometimes with infection.
glossary.dry gangrene: Ischaemic tissue death without infection: dry, black, painless and clearly demarcated.
glossary.wet gangrene: Gangrene with infection: moist, swollen, painful, foul-smelling, no clear edge.
glossary.gas gangrene: Life-threatening muscle infection by Clostridium perfringens producing gas in tissues.
glossary.clostridial myonecrosis: Another name for gas gangrene: muscle death caused by clostridial toxins.
glossary.Clostridium perfringens: Anaerobic, spore-forming Gram-positive rod that causes gas gangrene.
glossary.alpha-toxin: Lecithinase made by Clostridium perfringens that destroys cell membranes.
glossary.lecithinase: Enzyme that breaks down lecithin in cell membranes, killing cells.
glossary.necrosis: Death of cells or tissue from injury or loss of blood supply.
glossary.ischaemia: Inadequate blood supply to a tissue, starving it of oxygen.
glossary.demarcation: The visible line between dead and living tissue.
glossary.mummified: Dried out, shrunken and hard, as in dry gangrene.
glossary.crepitus: A crackling feeling under the fingers, here from gas in soft tissue.
glossary.subcutaneous emphysema: Gas or air trapped under the skin, felt as crackling.
glossary.PVD: Peripheral vascular disease: narrowing of the arteries to the limbs.
glossary.peripheral arterial disease: Atherosclerotic narrowing of the arteries supplying the legs.
glossary.ABPI: Ankle-brachial pressure index: ankle systolic pressure divided by arm systolic pressure.
glossary.CT angiography: CT with IV contrast showing the arteries and any blockage.
glossary.revascularisation: Restoring blood flow by angioplasty or bypass surgery.
glossary.debridement: Surgical or other removal of dead, infected tissue from a wound.
glossary.amputation: Surgical removal of a limb or part of a limb.
glossary.sepsis: Life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated response to infection.
glossary.lactate: Blood marker of poor tissue perfusion; above 4 mmol/L signals severe sepsis.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein: a blood marker of inflammation and infection.
glossary.co-amoxiclav: Amoxicillin with clavulanic acid, a broad-spectrum penicillin.
glossary.flucloxacillin: Narrow-spectrum penicillin active against Staphylococcus aureus.
glossary.piperacillin-tazobactam: Very broad-spectrum IV penicillin with a beta-lactamase inhibitor (Tazocin).
glossary.clopidogrel: Antiplatelet drug blocking the P2Y12 receptor, used in vascular disease.
glossary.atorvastatin: Statin that lowers cholesterol and stabilises atherosclerotic plaque.
glossary.necrotising fasciitis: Rapidly spreading infection of the fascia with pain out of proportion; a surgical emergency.
glossary.multi-organ failure: Failure of two or more organ systems, often from sepsis.

technique.stem: A 72 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has had a black right fourth toe for 2 weeks. Over 2 days the toe and forefoot have become swollen, moist and blistered with a foul-smelling purulent discharge. There is no clear boundary between the necrotic and healthy tissue. She feels unwell. Her temperature is 38.6°C, pulse rate 112 bpm and BP 104/66 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about necrotic tissue: decide dry, wet or gas.
Necrosis plus moisture, pus, odour, fever and no demarcation: infected necrotic tissue.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Wet gangrene.**

elim: An arterial ulcer is a punched-out wound, not a black infected toe.
Cellulitis does not cause black necrotic tissue.
Dry gangrene is dry, painless, demarcated and afebrile.
Venous ulcers are shallow, medial and not necrotic.

steps.x: **E. Wet gangrene.** Black + moist + pus + fever + no line = wet.

technique.stem: A 70 year old man has a black, dry, shrivelled left big toe with a clear line of demarcation. It is painless. He has smoked for 50 years and has calf claudication at 50 m. Foot pulses are absent. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?

steps.x: The **initial** test for suspected dry gangrene.

clues: black, dry, shrivelled left big toe
steps.x: Dry gangrene from arterial disease; no infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Examine viability, then **ABPI**: below 0.8 supports dry gangrene.

elim: No fever or sepsis; cultures are not the first test.
Gold standard to map the blockage, after ABPI.
MRI looks for osteomyelitis, not arterial supply.
Dry gangrene is not infected.

steps.x: **A. ABPI.** First-line for dry gangrene; CT angiography next.

technique.stem: A 74 year old man has dry gangrene of his right second and third toes. Vascular surgeons have reviewed him and planned revascularisation. He takes metformin and ramipril only. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
technique.q: Which drug combination should be started for his underlying vascular disease?

steps.x: Secondary prevention for the vascular disease behind dry gangrene.
Arterial disease, not on antiplatelet or statin, high cholesterol.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Clopidogrel** (antiplatelet) plus **atorvastatin** (lipids).

elim: Aspirin plus dipyridamole is an old stroke regimen, not PAD first-line.
BP drugs do not treat the atheroma; he is normotensive on ramipril.
Anticoagulation alone is not standard for PAD.
Warfarin is not indicated; ezetimibe is not first-line.

steps.x: **C.** Clopidogrel + atorvastatin for every gangrene patient with vascular disease.

technique.stem: A 68 year old man with peripheral arterial disease has a black, dry, painless left big toe. There is a sharp line between the black toe and the pink skin of the foot. He has no fever.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation for the sharp line?
o: Bacterial gas tracking along tissue planes
Mummification of dead tissue beside perfused viable tissue

steps.x: A mechanism question: why is dry gangrene demarcated?
Dry gangrene with no infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dead tissue **desiccates**; adjacent tissue stays **perfused**, so the edge is sharp.

elim: Gas tracking is gas gangrene and spreads, not demarcates.
Clostridial toxin is gas gangrene.
Immune complexes cause vasculitis, not this line.
Liquefaction is a feature of wet gangrene.

steps.x: **D.** Dry = mummified dead tissue next to living perfused tissue.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man has had darkening of his right big toe for 4 weeks. He has smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 50 years. The toe is black, shrivelled, hard and painless. There is a clear line between the black toe and the healthy skin. There is no discharge. His temperature is 36.6°C.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Black, shrivelled, painless, clearly demarcated and uninfected tissue in a heavy smoker is dry gangrene.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a black toe.

clues: smoked 30 cigarettes a day for 50 years
steps.x: Mummified, demarcated, no infection, smoker.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dry gangrene.**

elim: An ulcer is a wound, not a whole mummified toe.
No cold exposure is described.
Gas gangrene follows trauma with crepitus and sepsis.
Wet gangrene is moist, painful, foul and poorly demarcated.

steps.x: **B. Dry gangrene.** Dry, black, painless, clear line.

practice.stem: A 63 year old woman with type 2 diabetes has a 3 day history of a painful, swollen left foot. Her left third toe has been black for a month. The forefoot is now red, moist and blistered with a foul-smelling discharge and no clear edge to the necrosis. Her temperature is 38.9°C, pulse rate 116 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Infected necrotic tissue that is moist, foul, painful and poorly demarcated, with sepsis, is wet gangrene. Dry gangrene is uninfected and demarcated.

steps.x: Diagnosis: dry, wet or gas gangrene?
Necrotic toe now infected, with fever and raised lactate.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Wet gangrene** with sepsis.

elim: Cellulitis does not produce black necrotic tissue.
Charcot foot is a warm, deformed foot without necrosis or sepsis.
Dry gangrene has no infection and a clear line.
Gout causes a hot joint, not necrosis and pus.

steps.x: **E. Wet gangrene.** It is an emergency.

practice.stem: A 34 year old man cut his foot on a rusty nail while gardening 2 days ago. He now has severe pain in the foot, far worse than its appearance suggests. The skin is discoloured with bullae and a foul-smelling discharge. Light palpation produces a crackling sensation. His temperature is 39.2°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 92/58 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Trauma, pain out of proportion, bullae, foul discharge, crepitus and sepsis are gas gangrene (Clostridium perfringens).

steps.x: Diagnosis after a penetrating wound.

clues: cut his foot on a rusty nail
far worse than its appearance suggests
steps.x: Trauma, disproportionate pain, bullae and **crepitus**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Gas gangrene** (clostridial myonecrosis).

elim: Cellulitis does not crackle or cause bullae with sepsis this fast.
DVT causes calf swelling, no crepitus or discharge.
Dry gangrene is painless and uninfected.
Tetanus causes muscle spasm and trismus, not crepitus.

steps.x: **D. Gas gangrene.** Wound + crepitus + pain out of proportion.

practice.stem: A 45 year old woman had a deep laceration to her thigh in a road traffic collision 36 hours ago. She now has severe thigh pain, swelling, bronze discolouration and bullae. Her temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 128 bpm and BP 88/54 mmHg. Gas gangrene is suspected.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on palpation of the thigh?
practice.e: Gas in the soft tissues (subcutaneous emphysema) produces crepitus on light palpation, the classic sign of gas gangrene.

steps.x: A finding question: name the condition, then its sign.
Trauma then myonecrosis with gas.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Gas in tissue planes: **crepitus**.

elim: Pain is severe; sensation is not the key finding.
Septic shock does not give bounding limb pulses as a sign.
Pitting oedema is non-specific and not the classic sign.
A pulsatile mass suggests a false aneurysm.

steps.x: **C. Crepitus.** Gas gangrene crackles.

practice.stem: A 79 year old man has peripheral arterial disease and type 2 diabetes. Over 3 weeks his left fourth and fifth toes have turned black. They are cold and dry with no swelling or discharge. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 74 bpm and BP 146/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of the toes?
practice.e: Dry ischaemic gangrene is clearly demarcated from healthy tissue. The other findings mean infection: wet or gas gangrene.

steps.x: A finding question: which type of gangrene is this?
Ischaemic, dry and uninfected: dry gangrene.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Dry gangrene gives a **clear line of demarcation**.

elim: Crepitus is gas gangrene.
Discharge means wet gangrene.
Moist blistering means wet gangrene.
Spreading erythema means infection.

steps.x: **A.** Dry gangrene = demarcated.

practice.stem: A 71 year old woman with wet gangrene of her right foot has become drowsy. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 132 bpm, BP 78/44 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 93% breathing air.
practice.q: Which complication of her gangrene has developed?
practice.e: Fever, tachycardia, hypotension, raised lactate and AKI in wet gangrene is sepsis with organ failure, a recognised complication.

steps.x: Complication of gangrene.
Infected source, fever, shock and organ dysfunction.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Sepsis** heading to multi-organ failure.

elim: No trigger, rash or wheeze.
No cardiac history or pulmonary oedema; there is fever.
No bleeding is described.
PE does not explain a high fever from an infected foot.

steps.x: **E. Sepsis.** Then Sepsis Six and source control.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man has severe pain in his right leg 1 day after a deep puncture wound. The skin is discoloured with bullae and crepitus is felt. His temperature is 38.8°C, pulse rate 120 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. The surgeon wants imaging to confirm gas in the tissues while theatre is prepared.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: In suspected gas gangrene, an X-ray shows gas in the soft tissues. It must not delay emergency debridement.

steps.x: Imaging to show gas in tissue.
Suspected gas gangrene.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **X-ray** for soft tissue gas, plus CRP and lactate.

elim: Maps arterial blockage, not gas.
D-dimer is for VTE.
Irrelevant to infection.
Looks for DVT, not gas.

steps.x: **D. Plain X-ray.** Gas in soft tissues.

practice.stem: A 74 year old man has dry gangrene of his left second toe. He smokes and has claudication. His temperature is 36.7°C. The vascular surgeon wants to know where his arteries are blocked before planning revascularisation.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
practice.e: CT angiography is the gold standard to identify the arterial blockage. The ABPI is already known and only gives severity.

steps.x: Which test shows where the blockage is?
Severity known (ABPI 0.41); anatomy needed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CT angiography.**

elim: Already done; it does not locate the lesion.
No sepsis.
Shows bone and gas, not arteries.
Dry gangrene is not infected.

steps.x: **C. CT angiography**, gold standard.

practice.stem: A 77 year old woman has dry gangrene of her right big toe with a clear line of demarcation. There is no fever, discharge or spreading redness. Her right ABPI is 0.44. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 80 bpm and BP 152/86 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Topical antiseptic and review in 3 months
practice.e: Dry gangrene needs urgent vascular referral for revascularisation, with amputation of non-viable tissue. There is no infection to treat.

steps.x: Initial management of dry gangrene.

clues: no fever, discharge or spreading redness
steps.x: Uninfected ischaemic necrosis with critical ischaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent vascular surgery referral** for revascularisation.

elim: Compression is dangerous with a low ABPI.
Not standard first-line care.
There is no infection.
Waiting 3 months risks limb loss.

steps.x: **E.** Dry gangrene = urgent vascular referral.

practice.stem: A 68 year old man with diabetes has a black, moist, swollen left foot with pus, a foul smell and no clear demarcation. He has no drug allergies. His temperature is 38.7°C, pulse rate 114 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: IV co-amoxiclav and urgent surgical review
practice.e: Wet gangrene is an emergency: immediate IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (co-amoxiclav) and urgent surgical review for debridement or amputation.

steps.x: Initial management, in a septic patient.
Wet gangrene with early sepsis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IV co-amoxiclav** plus urgent surgery.

elim: Secondary prevention, not emergency care.
Oral treatment is inadequate for wet gangrene.
Far too slow for an emergency.
Dressings do not treat spreading infection.

steps.x: **A.** Wet = IV antibiotics + urgent surgery.

practice.stem: A 40 year old man has severe pain, bullae and crepitus in his left leg 2 days after a crush injury. His temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 130 bpm and BP 84/50 mmHg. X-ray shows gas in the soft tissues.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Emergency surgical debridement and IV piperacillin-tazobactam
IV fluids and observe for 24 hours
MRI of the leg before any surgery
practice.e: Gas gangrene needs emergency surgical debridement, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin-tazobactam) and ICU care.

steps.x: Management of a septic patient with gas in tissue.
Gas gangrene with septic shock.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Emergency debridement**, IV pip-taz, ICU.

elim: Oral antibiotics are inadequate.
Never instead of surgery.
Delay is fatal.
Imaging must not delay theatre.

steps.x: **B.** Gas gangrene = theatre now.

practice.stem: A 30 year old man has gas gangrene of his calf after a contaminated wound. His pulse rate is 126 bpm and BP 90/56 mmHg. There is crepitus and severe pain out of proportion to the skin changes. Gram stain of the tissue shows large Gram-positive rods.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the muscle destruction?
practice.e: Clostridium perfringens alpha-toxin, a lecithinase, causes myonecrosis and gas, giving crepitus and disproportionate pain.

steps.x: Mechanism of myonecrosis in gas gangrene.
Clostridium perfringens.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Alpha-toxin**, a lecithinase.

elim: Vasculitis mechanism.
Toxic shock (Staph or Strep) mechanism.
Clostridium tetani: spasm, not myonecrosis.
Thrombosis gives dry ischaemic gangrene, not gas.

steps.x: **A.** C. perfringens alpha-toxin = lecithinase.
